simply working by the day receiving $5 a day and expenses. But, that is not the worst. Take the case of J. Franklin, services, 193 days at $5, 9 days at $4, board and lodging, $425.55 ; cabs, $3.75 ; pull-maps, $276.50 ; street cars, $8.45 ; tips, $6 ; sundries, $4.25 ; making a total of $1,651.80. This gentleman takes $6 of the people's money with which to tip waiters, &c. Next we have R. W. Hillyard, services 147 days at $5 ; 6 days at $4 ; 4 22-30 m. at $1,000; board and lodging, $425.50; bus, $4.40 ; coal oil. $2.24 ; fares, $44.55 ; hand basins, $8.03 ; livery, $135.55; provisions for immigrants, $5.85 ; pullmans, $235 ; street cars, $11.45 ; telegrams, $2.70 ; tips $27.70 ; transfers, $4.20; sundries, $2.03, making a total of $2,074.87. This gentleman spends $27.70 for tips, but that is not the worst Geo. A. Johnston receives pay for services 125 days at $5 ; 1 day at $4 ; 4 22-30 m. at $1,000 ; board and lodging, $481.80 ; cabs, $2.25 ; fares, $27 ; pullmans, $305.50 ; provisions for immigrants, $3.55 ; telegrams, $2.80 ; tips, $11 ; wash basins, $1.50 ; sundries, $4.04 ; making a total of $1,875.11. L. Kelioe receives pay for services 18 days at $5 ; 19 days at $4 ; board and lodging, $71 ; pullmans, $56 ; street cars, 70 cents ; uniform cap, $5 or in all $298.70. Mr. W. D. Scott receives for board and lodging, $532.50; baggage transfer, $7.75; cabs, $14.75; map, $1; pullmans, $68.75 ; street cars, $9.25 ; tips, $5.25 ; making a total of $639.25. The next is Mr. G. B. Smart. Mr. Smart is set down as a salaried officer at $1,400 looking after pauper children, and here are his expenses : Board and lodging, $465.38 ; baggage transfers, $8.50; cab and bus fares, $56.40 ; cigars, $7. The government have to furnish him with cigars. He charged them up to the government. He took the people's money bought cigars and smoked them with his heels up on the seat of a pullman because he is allowed $107.85 for pullmans. Fares, $48.78 ; livery, $264.75 ; postage; $3.76 ; printing cards, $2.60 ; pullmans, $107.85; street cars, $19.20 ; telegrams, $11.55 ; telephones, $4.10; tips, $23.95; sundries, $1.87 ; making, a .total of $1,025.69. lie takes $23 of the people's money with which to tip waiters and others and this added to $7 for cigars, makes $30. of the people's money expended in this way, yet, this vote is supposed to be for immigration purposes. Of what assistance is it towards bringing immigrants into this country to pay $7 to Mr. Smart to buy cigars and $23 to give in tips to waiters ? Is it the intention of the hon. Minister of the Interior to continue this policy under his management of the department ? Is he going to allow the people's money to be frittered away in this shape ? If so, we had better say we will give up importing immigrants at all.

Hear, hear.
* Mr. COCHRANE. My friends opposite approve of it and say it is all right for a

civil servant to put his hand into the treasury and take out $7 and buy cigars and give $23.50 in tips to waiters. Hundreds of thousands of dollars are frittered away in that way. Every servant in connection with this department at Halifax, Montreal or Quebec is allowed three uniform suits during the season, and two or three caps, running into $100 a year besides salary and liberal expenses. Surely the minister will reform the policy of the government unless he approves, which as an honest man he cannot do, of the conduct of the department. No wonder he is asking an increased amount, adding to the civil service list and appointing friends. I could point out agencies in the United States where some of these officials receive $6,000 and $7,000 between salary and expenses, holding office at Detroit, Milwaukee, &c. It is all detailed in the Auditor General's Report. Surely the minister can run the department and get as efficient service for one quarter the money that is spent here as is shown by the Auditor General's Report for last year. Let the minister look at the item of pullman car fares. Most members of parliament, or at least a great many of them, in travelling from Ottawa to Toronto do not occupy pullman cars, but here a civil servant if he travels must have a pullman car charged to the people of this country. I think it is time the minister would call a halt and ask these gentlemen to pay for their own cigars and tips to waiters out of their own pockets, instead of out of the pockets of the people. I trust the minister, before the vote passes, will cut down the item as it can be cut down, and still have a better service than we have had in the past for the money voted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not had the time or opportunity to go over the actual working of the department since taking hold, but I can quite accept the criticism made, which is perfectly in order, and I shall certainly accept the duty laid on me when I ha've the opportunity to go into the administration of the department, and do the best I can to secure reasonable economy, accompanied of course by efficiency. I am not able to say just how it comes that these expenditures have been made and all that astonishes me is that the books show these accounts have been paid after having passed the lynx-eyed Auditor General.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Because they are certified by some officer of your department and the Auditor General is obliged to pay.
I expect you know well enough.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I only wish he would be as good with some accounts I know to be perfectly honest but which he is not willing to pass.
Never mind the Auditor General. Let us know what the minister is going to do himself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On inquiry of the officer of the department here in regard to one or two of those expenditures, I find that Mr. Blair is employed as an inspector of the immigrant children and this expense of inspection is paid by the imperial government. There is an arrangement whereby when children come out under official supervision they have to be officially inspected every year and for this inspection, except the first inspection, the imperial government pay, so that the expense, as I am given to understand, is a mere form ; although appearing in our report as charged upon our department it really represents a payment to us by the imperial government. The same is true in regard to a Mr. Hiliyard, whose name is mentioned there in regard to the same employment. In reference to the use of pullman cars I understand that this use has mostly taken place in returning from the conduct of immigrants out west. We start the immigrants from Montreal or Ottawa in charge of a guide so to speak, who accompanies the party to Winnipeg and sees to their distribution over the branch lines there and then comes back. The trip from Winnipeg to Ottawa occupies two days and nights, and any one travelling on the train must either use a pullman or sit up, and I think it is generally considered it is necessary for even a government official to sleep ; it is upon that ground I believe that these pullman expenses are paid. As to the use of pulhnans between here and Toronto we pay, as the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has said, about $5 a day. I take it as cheaper to pay the cost of a pullman from here to Toronto and have the officer travel at night than have him lose $5 worth of daylight in making the same trip so that while I do not at all care for extra luxuries-and certainly some of these expenses will bear very careful inquiry-I think there is sometimes an appearance of economy that is not economy and an appearance of extravagance that is not extravagance.
Will the minister tell how many children these three inspectors inspected ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The number on the inspection list at present is about 1,100.
Where are the homes situated that these children are furnished to and distributed from ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are mostly distributed amongst the farmers.
The minister must know-if he does not he ought to-that they come to homes at first in Belleville, Peterborough and so forth and then are distributed to the farmers from the homes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There are 13 receiving homes in this country and they come from about 115 in the old country.

Mr, COCHRANE. Are there any in central Ontario, Belleville, Peterborough, &c., that distribute the children that these gentlemen inspect ? My opinion is that that inspectro"n is a perfect fraud on the country. The hon. gentleman says there is something to be said ; there was a good deal to be said in connection with such an expenditure when the Conservative party was in power.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman says ' hear, hear.' if he would mind what he is doing and not be so quick with his ' hear, hear,' and his simple grin and pay-more attention to the conduct of public affairs it would be better for him.
Hear, hear.

There is another gentleman with his ' hear, hear.' I did not expect to see the hon. gentleman in the House; he said he would resign, but I knew that he would not be very resigning if he could get out of it.
How are you on the question of skimmed milk ?

How are you ? 1 will let you know if you repeat that to me outside" the House. If you had any manhood about you, you would not do it. You come outside the House and say that to me, and I will let you know. I was saying to the minister that when the administration that I used to support was making economical expenditures, there were men then on this side of the House who would keep us all night talking over a few dollars of expenditure. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen to say ' hear, hear,' and smile, but they do not realize that they are spending the people's money for tips and cigars. East year or the year before Walker's whisky was furnished to the Minister of Agriculture. The poor people of the country are earning by the sweat of their brow the money to pay the taxes which hon. gentlemen opposite are spending. I do not object to any expenditure for the good of the country, but 1 object to officials travelling in special cars. When we were in power hon. gentlemen opposite talked from morning till night about the iniquity of Sir John Macdonald travelling in a special car; yet I have heard on good authority that the late Minister of the Interior travelled about the Northwest with his father and brother in a private car, for which, I suppose, the country is paying, in the section of country where I live I venture to say that not one of these gentlemen ever inspected one of the homes that the hon. Minister of the Interior speaks of. They have been inspected by ladies ; but so far as these gentlemen are concerned, unless more has been done in other sections of the country than in that section, the inspection of these children is a perfect fraud
on the people, and the money is worse than uselessly expended.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can only say that the officers of the department reiterate that the inspection has been made every year.
I emphatically contradict the statement.
Would the minister tell us when the two assistant inspectors vv ere appointed ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Blair is not now employed. Mr. Smart is, and has been a permanent inspector, and he is assisted at the present time by Mr. Hillyard.
Mr. Scott, the Commissioner of Immigration, told us in the committee that there were three-Mr. Smart, Mr. Hillyard and Mr. Corry.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Corry was appointed quite recently in Manitoba.

Last year, according to the report, there were 2,204 children, of whom 1,188 were in four of Dr. Barnar-co's homes. This year we have only 1,142 children, yet there are one or two additional inspectors. Under these circumstances, I do not think that increase can be very well justified. Even if the inspection has to be paid for in the old country, that is no justification for wasting the money, because it gives us a bad name.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The difference in the number of children does not make very much difference in the work of inspection, inasmuch as they are scattered widely all over the country from ocean to ocean. It would be easy to show that it would not cost so much to inspect half a dozen children located in one school section as two separated in different counties.

But you had twice the number last year and only one inspector.
Mr. OLIVER, No ; there were two. Mr. Hillyard was acting as inspector last year.

Here is an item of some considerable importance on which I would like to have a fe\V more details : Commissioner Smith, expenses for land guides, interpreters, temporary agents, clerks, travelling expenses, ma-ttresses, provisions, and all expenses connected with locating immigrants on land, $130,000.
I understand from the minister that while we spend on immigration from the United States some $30,000 on salaries we spend only $18,000 in Great Britain and Ireland.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the United States $31,000 and in Great Britain and Ireland $19,000.

Although I realize that the class of immigrants from the United States is a very good class, still I think it would be better to put forth greater efforts in the mother country. I do not think any class could equal the small tenant farmer class, the men who work their own farms in the mother country. We are not getting enough of them. If a larger amount were spent to get that particular class, we would get better results than we do from the expenditure in the United States.

The efforts of the department in the past have been, as they will be in the future, very strongly directed towards the object the hon. gentleman mentions. But the difficulty in securing the immigration of tenant farmers from the old country is that they are wanted in the old country just as much as they are here. I can assure him that no effort will be spared, but they are a class of people very conservative in their habits, if not in their politics, and will require to be attacked apparently from as yet an undiscovered point in order to secure them.
Does the hon. minister intend to continue the payment of $o per head to agents who bring in immigrants from the continent ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am given to understand that there is a contract for ten years. I cannot give the date at the moment, but it was entered into and the department would be bound by it.
A very bad contract.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Possibly. Of course the question of policy would always have to be considered.
Will you bring down that contract ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have it here but there are reasons why it should not be generally published. I shall be glad, however, to place it at the disposal of my hon. friend, on the understanding that it will not be made public.

I think it would be well if my hon. friend would give us the different contracts by virtue of which we are bound to pay a bonus to steamship companies or other tranportation companies on the carriage of immigrants.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is only the one.

I think the House is entitled to see that contact unless there be grave reasons of state why we should not. I assume that my hon. friend himself did not make that contract binding us for ten years to pay $5 a head on every immigrant from the continent. That is certainly a very con-demnable policy indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) says the country is bound for ten years. He is a lawyer and I am not, and I presume he means that we may be bound to make good a contract entered into by the government. I however, do not think that we are either morally or legally bound. The ex-M inis ter of Interior (Mr. Sifton) knew perfectly well that he had no authority to make any such contract. This parliament never authorized it. Beyond the period of one year for which money is voted, no minister can make a contract binding parliament. The thing would be monstrous. What is the use of parliament meeting once every twelve months if a minister, at his own whim, may appropriate the public money for ten years to come ? Hie present minister would be only doing his duty if he would cancel that contract and take care not to enter into any contract in the future beyond the period for which the money is voted I trust we shall have no more revelations of this kind. I trust that the present minister will have too much self-respect to enter into any other such contract. There is no use saying that we are bound by it for ten years. As a matter of fact we are not bound either legally or morally, and I trust that the hon. minister will see that the contract is cancelled at once. We can do very well without getting immigrants from the continent except from one or two special countries. The time has come when we can get all the immigrants we want without paying anything per head and we will get a better- class. The poorest kind o'f immigrant is the one you have to pay for. The man who will make a good citizen is the one whose only inducement to settle in this country is what the government offers in the way of land and what the country offers in the way of a fertile soil and healthy climate. And I trust that there will be no more of this bonus system, but that whatever obligation has been undertaken by the previous minister will be forthwith cancelled, and let men come to this country of their own free will. I do not see the need for filling up this country so hastily. Immigration, 1 think, is coming in with sufficient rapidity. Perhaps, even if it were not coming in so fast, we could take better care of those who do come, and the immigration would inure more to the benefit of the country. But, by all means let us cease giving bonuses to bring in a class of immigrants that have never proved as acceptable as those that have come in without government aid.
McLEaN. Is there any lawT on the statute-book which authorizes the Minister of the Interior to enter into this contract, or has he entered into it by virtue of his position ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I presume that the Minister of the Interior made the contract in

the belief tliat it was sound public policy and by virtue of bis authority as Minister of the Interior and as officer charged with the duty of inducing immigration.
Perhaps the minister has found the details of that expenditure of $130,000 ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amount directly expended under the authority of Mr. Smith, of the Winnipeg office, is $80,000. There are ether amounts that make up this total of $130,000.
There must be a lot of details.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can give the details for the $80,000. It will be observed we have been considering one end of this service, the inducing of settlers, but this has to do with the location of settlers.
Does the explanation the minister is about to give cover the current year to the end of this month or the coming year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The particulars I have are for the year ending June 30th, 1904.
But later on the minister will be able to give us the expenditure for the current year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think so. The expenditure during the year ending June 30th, 1904, was $76,087, which is about equal to the estimate we have made for the coming year $80,000. But the expenditure for the current year was larger than usual because items were paid that had been carried over-. That expenditure is covered by the supplementary vote for the current year, which has already passed the House. But expenditures in the ordinary way, have remained about the same. This expenditure was divided into these classes :
Miscellaneous, $333.
Interpreters-services and expenses, $2,066.
Cannot the hon. minister state the number of these ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have such details for the past years, but not for the coming year.
But it is on past experience, I presume, that you have based your present estimate ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. Travelling and living expenses of officials in the west for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1904, $8,401. There is another item, transportation and location of immigrants, $7,673. Some of these officials might possibly be included in some other items of expenditure in this service. The hon. member asked me for the salaries of the western officials for the coming year, but we are not able to give the item'for contingencies for the coming year.
I -was giving the particulars of the expenses for contingencies last year, $80,000. Miscellaneous, $333; interpreters' services and expenses, $2,566; land guides, $11,274 ; sundry services, carpenters, clerical assistance, temporary agents, $12,202 ; delegates expenses, $125; travelling and living expenses of officials in west, $8,401 ; uniforms, $2,099 ; advertising, $478 ; collection of exhibits, $8,309 ; equipment, bedding, utensils, &c., $5,013 ; provisions, $3,563 ; laundry, cleaning office, &c., $1,629 ; medical services, expenses, supplies, &c., $4,466 ; transportation and location of immigrants, $7,673 ; contingencies, Winnipeg agency, $4,371 ; contingencies outside service, agencies in west, $3,579 ; total, $76,081.
How is it that some of the interpreters are getting $600 a year and other $1,200 ?
It depends somewhat on the length of service of the interpreter, and somewhat on the importance of the service.
Are the officers whose names the hon. gentleman read engaged the whole year round ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, on fixed salaries. The item for interpreters and land guides includes other people than the salaried officers whose names I read. The land guides are employed temporarily, by the day.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The officials whose salaries will come out of the $80,000 are those in the west who are engaged in the work of locating settlers.
I suppose their expenses also were paid ? Can the minister give the expenditure under that head ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The expenses are paid out of the vote for contingencies and general expenditure, and it cannot well be given for the different individuals.
Each man would have to make a return to the department of his expenses, and I should think the figures would be there showing each man's account with all the details.

There is another matter that seems strange, to which I wish some explanation. The Report of the Minister of Interior, page 166, gives the deportations at 270, the same report on page 169 gives the deportations at 85, in the same year [DOT] while Mr. Scott, in his evidence before the committee the other day, gave the numbers at 157. To my question at a pre-1 vious period of the session, the Prune Mm-i ister stated that there had bee* deported | '559 There seems to be a great deal of I confusion in the figures. I would like the ! minister to explain the discrepancies.
i Mr. OLIVER. I am informed that the ! figures do not cover the same periods, nor 'do thev relate to the same matters.

I will read the question and answer :
1.	How many immigrants were deported from this country during the fiscal year 1904, and up to the 1st of February. 1905 ?
2.	What were the nationalities ?
3.	What was the cause of their being deported ?
4.	How many were deported for disease, and for what disease ?
5.	How many because they were liable to become paupers ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
1. During the fiscal year, 1903-4, 359.
That is a straight answer to a straight question. Now I would like some explanation of these divergent figures. I think our public documents ought to be reliable, and a man could quote either of these three figures and say he was quoting official documents.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is impossible to give an answer off-hand. I am informed that the figures do not cover the same periods.

It covered the fiscal year 1903-4. That is what the annual report covers.
Mr. OLIVER, l understand the hon. member to say that the question was : \Vhat were the deportations for the fiscal year and up to the end of February, and that the answer was as to the number for the fiscal year.

I have the two answers here. I only read one of them, but I have the other as well : .
From the 1st July, 1904, to the 1st February 1905, 387 were deported.
I will send it over to my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What was the question which the hon. gentleman said was answered differently from this ?
I have your report. If you will turn to page 106 you will find that in table 9 the number of persons deported is given as 270.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: During what period ?
I suppose during the fiscal year 1903-4, because that is the period covered by the report. Then, look at page 109. I might as well send over the evidence taken at the committee if you want it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is an evident disci epancy between the answer read by the premier and the statement in the blue-book, it is impossible at the moment to say where the error was, but we will take measures to verify the one statement or the other, and see which is correct.

The hon. minister has given us a statement this evening about large expenditures in the way of interpreters Mr. OLIVER.
and agents locating settlers. I cannot understand how that applies to one part of the country differently from another part. In the locality where I live the country is practically. settled for a radius of twenty-five miles. I never saw one of tfie gentlemen that the hon. minister has spoken of locating settlers. I do not think there ever was one in that locality, and I do not see why this is necessary in one part of the country and not in another.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As the hon. member knows, the locality in which he lives is sufficiently attractive to bring settlers without any special advertisement or effort, but where the attractions are not so great it is necessary to employ the services of agents to bring the settler and the country together.

I have reference to locating settlers after they come into the country. According to what I understand from the reports, these gentlemen are paid for locating settlers and for showing them around the country. They hire teams to take them out and see the land so as to get a location. I am positive that there never were any of these gentlemen in the locality where I live.

I understood from one of the gentlemen who was before the committee that these locating gentlemen who are such an expensive luxury got $2 a day from the government in cash, and that if a mail wanted one of them to show him the land so as to enable him to locate he would have to pay from $4 to $0 a day extra for a team. I' should think these gentlemen who are paid by the government should not be receiving that much from a poor man who goes out there to locate his home, and that he would not be called upon to pay for a team to go around the country. What benefit are these agents if they have to be paid every day for their travelling expenses ?
I should think that when the government paid them they would not be extorting money from people who employ them to assist them in locating land. Do* they have to have tips, too ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A team is necessary for the travelling of a person who is looking for land, and he gets the benefit of the transportation by means of the team as well as of the services of the land guide in finding the lines and looking them up in his location. It seems to me a very satisfactory method ot dealing with the question. I have heard no complaints either as to hardship towards intending settlers or dissatisfaction on their part. Any one who lias ever had occasion to go out to look for land in a new country will know that it is of the very greatest advantage to the new pioneer who does not understand the lines and stakes or the lay of the land to have an experienced and reliable man with him. They are certainly

all willing, as far as I know, to pay for their services.

There are two or three men in my locality who make a living by that sort of business. When a man is looking for land he goes and hires with these men and also hires his team. He drives them over the country, and the man who is looking for land pays him about $5 a day for the use of his team and his own services. That has been paid in every case by every settler who comes into the district where I live.
What amount was paid last year under the ten years' contract referred to a few moments ago ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Under the arrangement during the past three years the total sum paid has been $87,000 1 am informed roughly. That has been paid to the North Atlantic Trading Company, the organization with which the arrangement is made.
Is the amount on the increase ?
It was a little less last year and it is expected to be less next year; it is rather on the decrease.

Has the minister any information to give in regard to the North Atlantic Trading Company. Who are the parties interested? It owns no ships and is not a regular shipping company. At the time the Doukhobors came to this country I tlfink $48,000 was paid to that same company. Does my hon. friend know anything about the company, who constitute it and what is its character generally ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I believe that it is an organization of steamship companies and it is quite possible to place at the disposal of my hon. friend all the information in regard to it. There is no Canadian reason why it should not be entirely public, but if the company is to continue its operations there are reasons why the facts should not be published outside of Canada. If the members will be satisfied with an opportunity of examining the question for themselves individually, we will be very glad to place all information at their disposal and if they insist it will have to be made a public document and open to the world, but our policy would be, if it is intended to continue the operation of the company, that is should not at the present time be made public.

I think it is a strong reason why the items should be more in detail for immigration purposes as pointed out by the members for Lennox (Mr. Uriah Wilson) and Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). Here the government enters into a ten years' contract without any consultation with the House at all. If an item had been placed in the estimates for payment to steamship companies, or rather steamship agents, for inducing farmers to come to Canada, a fixed amount in a separate column, then the minister would be entitled to give the House some information as to how that money is expended, but here a contract has been entered into and the House has no opportunity of discussing that item. It seems to me to be a pretty general policy and a policy that I think ought to be looked into.
I agrfce with the statement of the member for Lennox, that the details should be given in order that the House should be better informed on these items, as the money is being voted from time to time.

A good deal of the criticism which has come from this side of the House with regard to this item has been directed towards the expense, alleged to be unnecessary, in many instances, of providing salaries and expenses for the numerous agents of the department; and towards the classes of immigrants being brought to this country. As bearing upon those two points and generally upon the subject of immigration of farm labour into Canada, I ask the attention of the minister for a moment in regard to a private immigration scheme which is in operation in my own county of Prince Edward, Ont., with very beneficial results. A Mr. R. J. Crothers, a farmer in my county, having had correspondence with certain British immigration agencies,
I think in the first instance with one, of which Lord Aberdeen is the head, was joined by his neighbours, with a view of continuing the immigration of that class of immigrants. They formed an association amongst themselves-farmers who required farm help-and upon .payment of a nominal fee each farmer becomes a member of that association. As he requires farm help he makes application to the secretary stating the class of help he requires, the wages he is prepared to pay, whether or not he will advance the passage money, and it is understood in all cases that he is hiring for one year. These particulars are sent to the old country with a statement as to whether a married man is required or not. Then the associations in the old country with whom Mr. Crothers has communication send out the man, guaranteeing that he is a decent man and of the best class. In this way, since this private scheme has been in operation in Prince Edward county and in Hastings, an adjoining county, some 350 men have been brought out, chieffy from the north of England and south of Scotland. I have met many of these men and I am quite certain they are of the very best class, especially adapted to agricultural labour because that was their calling before coming here and they are especially selected In regard to qualification by the home associations. These men and their families amount to about 600 souls, that this private association has already brought out and placed

with the farmers of those two counties. When the man is sent out he is met at the station by Mr. Crothers and immediately taken to the farm of the farmer whose employ he is to enter. He knows before he leaves the old country to whom he is going, by what route, he is met on his arrival and taken to the farmer and knows especialy exactly what he is to get, and in ail cases he is engaged for at least a year. It appears to me that if the government would see fit to appoint such men as 'Mr. Crothers, men of substance with a reputation in their own locality and having the confidence of the people amongst whom they live, being-farmers themselves and not adventurers, not people seeking a job, but people responsible to the farmers with whom these men are placed, immensely satisfactory results might be expected. If there is one difficulty facing the farmers of Ontario today it is the problem of farm labour, and I think this, one very excellent method by which that growing need may be very largely, very effectually and very satisfactorily supplied, if the government would accord to people in the position of Mr. Crothers, something in the nature of official recognition by appointing him as an agent, the proper sort of men would be obtained. Of course the success of the scheme would lie absolutely in the class of men who would act as agents and none but the best men should be employed. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister with the view of having it receive his best consideration, and that he may decide whether such a policy as that could not with good effect be adopted. Here is an instance in which to my personal knowledge it has worked excellently. I know of no other means by which that body of men could have been brought into that locality.

be will say, carried. Doubtless he never dreamed till he came here that he had anything to do with the expenditure of the country, he thought that was something the ministers had to attend to. But I tell him that is not what his constituents expect him to do. They sent him here to watch and criticise closely the expenditure of the country, and to take ins share of the responsibility for all expenditures that are made. Now I find no fault with the minister with regard to this contract, because I admit it was not a contract of his making. But he must understand that he has a duty to perform with respect to this contract, lie lias the right to cancel it, and he must take the first opportunity of having this contract cancelled, no matter who is hurt, unless he comes down to parliament and gets that contract ratified before he makes any expenditure. Let the members of this House say whether that contract is to be validated or not, whether that money is to be expended. I say without hesitation that I do not think we are called upon, nor that it is in the interest of the country that we should hold out inducements of this kind to bring immigrants from European countries. There are certain European countries from which we are delighted to receive immigrants, but there are others from which we do not want to get-immigrants at all.
I am afraid that the most desirable immigrants from the continent of Europe come to us in the smaller numbers. There is a larger immigration, I believe, from countries where the immigrants are less desirable. I have made my statement as plain as I possibly couid make it and I am going to look for a better administration in the future of this department than we have had in the past. I am going to look for economy, I am going to look for a fair, honest administration, and I am going to hope that the department of immigration will not presume as much as they have done in the past, that they will not imagine that they are the masters of the country when they are simply doing the work that parliament pays them for doing. I say this in no disrepectful sense at all. I do not wish to reflect upon the department, but I say that members of parliament are entitled to some consideration and that they should not be ignored whilst their constituents throughout the country hold them responsible for the public expenditures. I shall not make that proposition this year hut if we should be fortunate enough to meet in another year I will bring this whole matter up. and if in the future another request of this kind comes before us. and I shall be in the House, I will deem it my duty to test the House on that question.

speechtext: It is for the observatory built on the Experimental Farm. The item for the purchase of instruments is $7,500. The chief item is for a meridian circuit, estimated to cost $5,000. The balance will provide for various optical and other instruments.
What is the diameter of the lens in the telescope there ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not able to say offhand, but I am informed 15 inches.

It lias always seemed to me that we did not show the highest wisdom in not getting a larger and better instrument when we were getting one at all.
Costs of litigation, $11,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is the same as last year. It is to provide for miscellaneous items of litigation that will happen in the best regulated families.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: It was understood that when we got a Solicitor General there would be no money paid for outside lawyers. Was the whole amount spent last year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In 1901-2, $2,938 were spent ; in 1902-3, $7,336 ; in 1903-4, $11,000.
Keewatin-maintenance of lunatics, $2,000.
Why does the Dominion government support these lunatics 7

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Because Keewatin is not in the same position as a province, and the Dominion is responsible. These lunatics are accommodated in the asylum at Manitoba and the Dominion pays.
Maintenance of assay office, Vancouver, $11,000.
What revenue does the government get ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We realized from siftings and findings $1,091.02, and from special assays $7.50, making a total of $1,098.52. This made a net expenditure for the fiscal year ending June 30th, 1904, of $10,582.75.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Here is an increase of $5,000. Why is that ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is an expenditure entered upon a year or two ago for getting out a standard topographic map of the Dominion in sheets. The standard topographic map is intended to cover the southern portion of the Dominion, the west coast and part of the Yukon.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Has there been a distribution of those already issued ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The work is in progress. Some of the sheets have been completed.

I have seen one or two of these sheets, but I do not understand the system or design. A map is made of a section, but not divided according to ordinary requirements, as into provinces and so on. I cannot see what the usefulness of it is unless the maps are completed in some way, and I have not been able to get any information as to when the whole will be completed, or even when a province or any particular section will be ready.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As I understand, the plans were entered upon some time ago. The country is divided up into sections, and for each section one of these standard maps is made. By using these separate sheets the map of any district can be made up. A map of the whole country upon the scale chosen would be useless, as it would be too large to be displayed, but maps of portions of the country can be made up by using these sections.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: yjr. SPROULE. But what I point out is that the work is not completed, nor are we told when it will he completed, or when any portion of it will be completed. And the maps of sections seem to be made without any relation to each other. There should be some design in the matter, and it should be known when the work will probably be completed either wholly or in certain parts.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: ' There is a uniform design and the parts are being brought out in regard to such portions of the country that happen to be at the moment the most interesting. And, when complete, that part can be fitted in with the other parts whenever they are ready.
At what age of the world's history will it be completed ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That will depend on the generosity of iiarliament in providing money.
Who is doing the work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The geographical staff of the Interior Department, and they are doing it gradually according to their capacity. To order the completion of such an immense map in a short time would involve a much larger expenditure, possibly, than parliament would feel inclined to authorize. Besides, it might not be possible to find the necessary number of men with the particular qualifications required.	.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This seems to be simply to find employment for an unnecessarily large staff.

But the work should not be carried on in a merely aimless desultory fashion and with no idea when it is to be completed. This seems a merely childish arrangement from a business standpoint. For instance there is a map of part of the oil district-hut only a part. When will the rest be completed ? I tried to get that information, and could not learn whether it would he completed next year, or ten years hence or ever. Yet we are asked to vote money for this service. It seems like frittering away money.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give the information as to when it is expected to finish the map, but I can give information which will partly answer the hon. gentleman's question. Up to a few years ago the mapping of the Domiuon proceeded in a desultory fashion. For instance the (peninsula of Ontario, the most densely populated part of the Dominion had not been mapped as it should have been. The section from Windsor to London has now been mapped and the sheet issued. The Hamilton sheet will he ready in a week or two and the Guelph sheet is more than half prepared. Another sheet will cover the portion of the peninsula west of the line from Oakville on Lake Ontario to ColUngwood on Georgian bay. Another sheet includes nearly the whole of

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: New Brunswick. Another covers that portion of Ontario immediately east of the Manitoba boundary which will be traversed by the National Transcontinental Railway- this is practically finished. Another sheet covers that portion of Quebec from the Island of Orleans to Montreal, and Ontario and Quebec are well advanced.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where ate they printed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The drawings are made here, and the Toronto Lithographing Company prepare the copperplates and do the printing.
Have these been distributed to members ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not aware what arrangement has been made for distribution. But I may say that those that are published, if they have not been already distributed to members, will be distributed.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is understood that the Autonomy Bill will be taken up, the clause in relation to the boundaries of the constituencies.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.40 p.m.
